title: Plotly Graph Objects Cheatsheet
name: Plotly Graph Objects Cheatsheet
description: High-density syntax recall for plotly.graph_objects (plotly.py 6.8.0), focused on figure-centric trace and layout composition, subplot grid orchestration, custom annotations, shapes, and interactive events.

entries.title: Import graph_objects
entries.problem: Start a graph_objects workflow.
entries.trigger: When you need manual figure composition instead of a high-level interface.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = go.Figure()
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use go for traces and Figure, and make_subplots for subplot grids. This is the standard import pair.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting make_subplots when targeting multiple panels.

entries.title: Create an empty figure
entries.problem: Initialize a blank figure for manual trace assembly.
entries.trigger: When building a plot step-by-step.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: This is the most common base object in graph_objects. Add traces and layout afterward.
entries.common_bug: Assuming a blank figure has default axes, titles, or data.

entries.title: Create a figure with initial data
entries.problem: Start a figure from one or more trace objects.
entries.trigger: When the chart has a known base trace set.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(data=[
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="lines+markers", name="series")
])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: data accepts trace instances or trace dicts. This is the simplest object-oriented bootstrap.
entries.common_bug: Passing raw arrays to data instead of trace objects.

entries.title: Create a figure with layout only
entries.problem: Define presentation settings before data arrives.
entries.trigger: When a template or dashboard shell is created first.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(layout=go.Layout(title="Empty shell", template="plotly_white"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: layout can be provided up front. Add traces later.
entries.common_bug: Expecting layout-only figures to render meaningful content.

entries.title: Create an animated figure from frames
entries.problem: Build a figure with explicit animation frames.
entries.trigger: When animation structure must be controlled manually.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(
    data=[go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers")],
    frames=[
        go.Frame(data=[go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6])], name="f1"),
        go.Frame(data=[go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6])], name="f2"),
    ],
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: frames holds frame definitions used by sliders and updatemenus. Keep frame data small.
entries.common_bug: Creating frames without controls to step through them.

entries.title: Add a single trace
entries.problem: Attach one trace to an existing figure.
entries.trigger: When building a figure incrementally.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="lines+markers", name="line"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_trace is the standard single-trace method. It is row/col aware for subplot figures.
entries.common_bug: Adding a trace to the wrong subplot because row and col were omitted.

entries.title: Add multiple traces at once
entries.problem: Insert a batch of traces efficiently.
entries.trigger: When several series belong to the same figure update.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_traces([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A"),
    go.Bar(x=["a", "b", "c"], y=[4, 5, 6], name="B"),
])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_traces is useful for batch composition. It is cleaner than repeated add_trace calls.
entries.common_bug: Adding mismatched trace types without checking subplot compatibility.

entries.title: Update all traces
entries.problem: Apply a consistent patch to every trace.
entries.trigger: When standardizing appearance across a figure.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_traces([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers", name="A"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers", name="B"),
])
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=12, opacity=0.8))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: update_traces broadcasts a patch across matching traces. Combine with selector for precision.
entries.common_bug: Changing every trace when only one series should be affected.

entries.title: Update selected traces
entries.problem: Modify only traces that match a filter.
entries.trigger: When traces differ by type, name, or index.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="line"),
    go.Bar(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="bars"),
])
fig.update_traces(selector=dict(type="scatter"), line=dict(width=3))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: selector narrows the patch to trace subsets. This is safer than global updates.
entries.common_bug: Using a selector that matches no traces and silently changing nothing.

entries.title: Select traces for inspection
entries.problem: Pull out traces matching criteria.
entries.trigger: When code needs to inspect or modify only a subset.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="B"),
])
selected = fig.select_traces(selector=dict(type="scatter"))
print(len(list(selected)))
entries.minimal_notes: select_traces is useful for programmatic figure logic. It pairs well with update_traces.
entries.common_bug: Assuming select_traces returns a single trace instead of an iterable.

entries.title: Iterate over traces
entries.problem: Apply custom logic to every trace.
entries.trigger: When updates cannot be expressed as one patch.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="B"),
])
fig.for_each_trace(lambda t: t.update(visible=True))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: for_each_trace is the ergonomic loop helper. Use it for conditional styling.
entries.common_bug: Mutating traces while expecting return values from the callback.

entries.title: Create a basic subplot grid
entries.problem: Place multiple charts into one figure.
entries.trigger: When comparing related views in a dashboard-like layout.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="top"), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="bottom"), row=2, col=1)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: make_subplots returns a Figure with prepared subplot axes. Add traces with row and col.
entries.common_bug: Adding traces to a subplot grid without specifying row and col.

entries.title: Share x-axes across rows
entries.problem: Link x-axis zooming across stacked plots.
entries.trigger: When time alignment must stay synchronized.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=2, col=1)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: shared_xaxes keeps the x domain aligned. Use it for time-series panels.
entries.common_bug: Using separate x-axes when synchronized zoom is expected.

entries.title: Share y-axes across columns
entries.problem: Compare traces using the same y scale.
entries.trigger: When magnitudes must be visually comparable.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, shared_yaxes=True)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=2)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: shared_yaxes is important for consistent comparisons. It prevents misleading scale differences.
entries.common_bug: Comparing panels with different y scaling unintentionally.

entries.title: Add a secondary y-axis subplot
entries.problem: Overlay series with different units.
entries.trigger: When one subplot needs a right-side scale.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(specs=[[{"secondary_y": True}]])
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="left"), secondary_y=False)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="right"), secondary_y=True)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: secondary_y is only valid in xy subplots. Use it for heterogeneous units.
entries.common_bug: Adding a secondary axis without configuring specs correctly.

entries.title: Use mixed subplot types
entries.problem: Combine Cartesian, polar, 3D, and domain-based views.
entries.trigger: When one figure needs multiple visualization modalities.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=2, cols=2,
    specs=[[{"type": "xy"}, {"type": "polar"}],
           [{"type": "scene"}, {"type": "domain"}]]
)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatterpolar(r=[1, 2, 3, 4], theta=[0, 90, 180, 270]), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter3d(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], z=[7, 8, 9]), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Pie(labels=["A", "B"], values=[10, 20, 30]), row=2, col=2)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: specs controls subplot type per cell. Domain subplots are used for pie and similar traces.
entries.common_bug: Assigning a trace to the wrong subplot type.

entries.title: Control subplot spacing
entries.problem: Tune whitespace between panels.
entries.trigger: When figure density needs adjustment.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=2, horizontal_spacing=0.05, vertical_spacing=0.08)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=2)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=2, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=2, col=2)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use spacing controls before resorting to manual layout edits. Smaller gaps increase density.
entries.common_bug: Making panel gaps so small that labels overlap.

entries.title: Add subplot titles
entries.problem: Label each panel clearly.
entries.trigger: When a multi-panel figure needs immediate readability.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("Left panel", "Right panel"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=2)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: subplot_titles is the fastest panel labeling path. Use it for comparison layouts.
entries.common_bug: Repeating titles in both subplot_titles and layout title unnecessarily.

entries.title: Create inset axes
entries.problem: Overlay a zoomed-in subplot on top of another plot.
entries.trigger: When detail needs to be highlighted without a second page.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(insets=[{"cell": (1, 1), "l": 0.65, "b": 0.55, "w": 0.3, "h": 0.3}])
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[2.1, 2.2, 2.4], xaxis="x2", yaxis="y2"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Insets are for compact overlays. Keep the inset content focused.
entries.common_bug: Using an inset for too much data and obscuring the base plot.

entries.title: Update layout
entries.problem: Change figure-wide presentation properties.
entries.trigger: When titles, legends, and margins need final control.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(
    title="Production figure",
    template="plotly_white",
    width=900,
    height=500,
    margin=dict(l=40, r=20, t=60, b=40)
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: update_layout is the main figure styling entry. It supports recursive updates.
entries.common_bug: Overwriting layout settings accidentally when repeatedly calling update_layout.

entries.title: Configure title and subtitle
entries.problem: Add figure-level context.
entries.trigger: When the output needs a report-ready heading.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(text="Main title", x=0.5),
    template="plotly_white"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Title is usually configured in layout. Use x to center it when needed.
entries.common_bug: Using multiple competing title systems in one figure.

entries.title: Configure legend placement
entries.problem: Position and orient the legend cleanly.
entries.trigger: When default legend placement blocks data.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="B"),
])
fig.update_layout(
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, xanchor="right", x=1)
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Legend can be moved out of the plotting area. Horizontal legends are common in reports.
entries.common_bug: Leaving the legend inside a crowded plot and covering data.

entries.title: Set fonts globally
entries.problem: Enforce typography across the figure.
entries.trigger: When charts need consistent publication styling.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(font=dict(family="Arial", size=14, color="black"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: font affects titles, axes, and legend text. Use one project-wide font choice.
entries.common_bug: Mixing incompatible fonts between exported images and browser rendering.

entries.title: Set templates
entries.problem: Apply a reusable figure theme.
entries.trigger: When multiple charts need the same style baseline.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_white")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Templates reduce repeated layout code. They are preferred in production workflows.
entries.common_bug: Mixing template styling with many one-off overrides.

entries.title: Set figure size
entries.problem: Control width and height for notebooks or exports.
entries.trigger: When layout dimensions must be deterministic.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(width=1000, height=600)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Set size explicitly for consistent exports. Avoid relying on renderer defaults.
entries.common_bug: Ignoring the target aspect ratio until export time.

entries.title: Set margins and background
entries.problem: Adjust figure whitespace and canvas colors.
entries.trigger: When preparing figures for dashboards or slides.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_layout(
    margin=dict(l=30, r=30, t=50, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="white",
    plot_bgcolor="#F8F8F8"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: paper_bgcolor affects the whole canvas; plot_bgcolor affects the plotting area. Use both deliberately.
entries.common_bug: Making the plot background and paper background clash visually.

entries.title: Set hover behavior globally
entries.problem: Control hover behavior across traces.
entries.trigger: When interactive readouts need consistency.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: hovermode changes how hover labels are grouped. Unified hover is common for time series.
entries.common_bug: Using the wrong hovermode for dense multi-trace figures.

entries.title: Set drag mode
entries.problem: Configure how users interact with the plot.
entries.trigger: When panning or zooming behavior matters.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.update_layout(dragmode="zoom")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: dragmode can be tuned for exploration workflows. Default behavior depends on the renderer.
entries.common_bug: Accidentally setting dragmode in a way that blocks expected zooming.

entries.title: Update x-axis range and type
entries.problem: Control x-axis scale and visible window.
entries.trigger: When the axis must be linear, logarithmic, date-based, or range-limited.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_xaxes(type="log", range=[0, 100], title="Log x")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: update_xaxes is the cleanest axis API. Use it instead of raw layout edits.
entries.common_bug: Using log axes with zero or negative values.

entries.title: Update y-axis range and autorange
entries.problem: Adjust y-axis view and auto scaling.
entries.trigger: When zoom behavior or plot extents need control.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, 100], autorange=False, title="Value")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: autorange=False makes ranges deterministic. This is useful for dashboards.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to disable autorange when a fixed range is intended.

entries.title: Configure ticks explicitly
entries.problem: Control axis tick values and labels.
entries.trigger: When categories or milestones must appear exactly.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_xaxes(tickmode="array", tickvals=[1, 2, 3], ticktext=["one", "two", "three"])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: tickmode='array' gives full control. Use it for custom labeling.
entries.common_bug: Setting ticktext without matching tickvals.

entries.title: Add grid and zero lines
entries.problem: Improve axis readability and reference context.
entries.trigger: When precise comparisons require visual guides.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[-1, 0, 1], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=True, zeroline=True)
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, zeroline=True)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Grid and zero lines help with interpretation. Keep them subtle in production output.
entries.common_bug: Overpowering the data with heavy grid styling.

entries.title: Lock axis scale and aspect
entries.problem: Preserve equal scaling between x and y.
entries.trigger: When geometry must be visually accurate.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.update_yaxes(scaleanchor="x", scaleratio=1)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: scaleanchor is essential for equal-aspect plots. Use it for spatial or metric comparisons.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that equal-aspect scaling can distort layout expectations.

entries.title: Add an annotation
entries.problem: Label a specific point or region.
entries.trigger: When commentary must be embedded in the plot.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.add_annotation(x=2, y=1, text="Peak", showarrow=True, arrowhead=2)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_annotation is the direct way to place callouts. Use showarrow only when pointing matters.
entries.common_bug: Anchoring annotation coordinates to the wrong axis reference.

entries.title: Add a horizontal line
entries.problem: Mark a threshold across the full plot width.
entries.trigger: When a target, baseline, or limit must be visible.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.add_hline(y=2, line_dash="dash", line_color="red")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_hline is the fastest threshold marker. It is layout-aware and subplot-friendly.
entries.common_bug: Using a regular shape line when hline is simpler and clearer.

entries.title: Add a vertical line
entries.problem: Mark a key x position.
entries.trigger: When event times or cutoffs need emphasis.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.add_vline(x=2, line_dash="dash", line_color="blue")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_vline is ideal for event markers. Keep labels concise.
entries.common_bug: Drawing the line in the wrong axis space on subplot figures.

entries.title: Add a horizontal rectangle
entries.problem: Highlight a y-range band.
entries.trigger: When tolerance or target bands matter.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.add_hrect(y0=1.2, y1=2.2, fillcolor="green", opacity=0.2, line_width=0)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: hrect is useful for ranges and acceptable zones. Use low opacity.
entries.common_bug: Making the fill too opaque and hiding the traces.

entries.title: Add a vertical rectangle
entries.problem: Highlight an x-range band.
entries.trigger: When a time window or region needs emphasis.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.add_vrect(x0=1.2, x1=2.2, fillcolor="orange", opacity=0.2, line_width=0)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: vrect is the x-range companion to hrect. It is commonly used for windows and periods.
entries.common_bug: Using a shape instead of vrect when the intent is a range band.

entries.title: Add an arbitrary shape
entries.problem: Draw custom geometry beyond lines and rectangles.
entries.trigger: When the figure needs a precise overlay.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.add_shape(type="circle", x0=1.4, x1=2.0, y0=1.0, y1=2.0, line=dict(color="purple"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: add_shape covers custom overlays. Use coordinate references carefully.
entries.common_bug: Drawing shapes in paper coordinates when data coordinates were intended.

entries.title: Create a scatter trace
entries.problem: Plot markers or lines on Cartesian axes.
entries.trigger: When most 2D plots begin as a scatter trace.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="lines+markers", name="series"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scatter is the foundation trace for many XY figures. Use mode to control mark style.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting mode and getting the default trace appearance.

entries.title: Create a bar trace
entries.problem: Show categorical magnitudes.
entries.trigger: When values belong to named categories.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Bar(x=["A", "B", "C"], y=[4, 5, 6], name="bars"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Bar traces are the standard category comparison trace. Use orientation for horizontal bars.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that stacked or grouped behavior depends on layout barmode.

entries.title: Create a histogram trace
entries.problem: Bin raw numeric data directly in graph_objects.
entries.trigger: When the figure needs built-in frequency binning.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Histogram(x=[1, 2, 3], nbinsx=5))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Histogram bins data in the trace itself. This is useful for quick distributions.
entries.common_bug: Comparing histograms without controlling bin settings.

entries.title: Create a box trace
entries.problem: Show quartiles and outliers in one trace.
entries.trigger: When distribution shape is important.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Box(y=[4, 5, 6], name="box"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Box traces are concise summary traces. They work well in grouped figures.
entries.common_bug: Interpreting a box trace with too few observations as robust.

entries.title: Create a violin trace
entries.problem: Show distribution density with shape detail.
entries.trigger: When a box plot is too coarse.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Violin(y=[4, 5, 6], box_visible=True, meanline_visible=True, name="violin"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Violin traces expose distribution shape. Adding box_visible is common for production use.
entries.common_bug: Drawing too many violins and crowding the axis.

entries.title: Create a heatmap trace
entries.problem: Show matrix values in a 2D grid.
entries.trigger: When correlation or intensity matrices are needed.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(z=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], colorscale="Viridis"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Heatmaps are the main matrix trace. Control colorscale for readability.
entries.common_bug: Not labeling axes for matrix interpretation.

entries.title: Create a contour trace
entries.problem: Draw contour lines for a scalar field.
entries.trigger: When isolines are more useful than filled cells.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Contour(z=[[1, 2, 3], [3, 4, 5], [2, 5, 6]], contours_coloring="lines"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Contour is the line-based scalar field trace. Pair with heatmap only when needed.
entries.common_bug: Overcomplicating the contour settings for a simple overview.

entries.title: Create a surface trace
entries.problem: Render a 3D surface from a matrix.
entries.trigger: When a continuous response surface needs 3D display.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(z=[[1, 2, 3], [3, 4, 5], [2, 5, 6]]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Surface traces are intended for 3D scene figures. Keep meshes reasonably sized.
entries.common_bug: Using too many grid points and slowing rendering.

entries.title: Create a mesh3d trace
entries.problem: Render a triangular 3D mesh.
entries.trigger: When the object is defined by vertices and faces.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Mesh3d(
    x=[0, 1, 2, 0],
    y=[0, 0, 1, 2],
    z=[0, 2, 0, 1],
    i=[0, 0, 0, 1],
    j=[1, 2, 3, 2],
    k=[2, 3, 1, 3],
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Mesh3d is for volumetric surface meshes. Index arrays define faces.
entries.common_bug: Mismatching face indices and vertex counts.

entries.title: Create a 3D scatter trace
entries.problem: Plot points in 3D space.
entries.trigger: When three coordinates are required.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter3d(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], z=[7, 8, 9], mode="markers"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scatter3d belongs to scene subplots. It is the default 3D point trace.
entries.common_bug: Adding a 3D trace to a 2D subplot.

entries.title: Create a polar scatter trace
entries.problem: Plot radial and angular coordinates.
entries.trigger: When directional data must be shown in a circular frame.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatterpolar(r=[1, 2, 3, 4], theta=[0, 90, 180, 270], mode="lines+markers"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scatterpolar belongs in polar subplots. Keep angular units consistent.
entries.common_bug: Mixing degrees and radians without normalization.

entries.title: Create a geographic scatter trace
entries.problem: Plot points on a geographic projection.
entries.trigger: When lat/lon data must be displayed on a world map.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scattergeo(lat=[23.81, 22.36], lon=[90.41, 91.80], mode="markers"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scattergeo is the stable geographic point trace. Use it for map-based point data.
entries.common_bug: Swapping latitude and longitude columns.

entries.title: Create a choropleth trace
entries.problem: Shade regions by value.
entries.trigger: When region identifiers and values map to a geography.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Choropleth(
    locations=["USA", "CAN", "MEX"],
    z=[7, 8, 9],
    locationmode="ISO-3",
    colorscale="Viridis"
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Choropleth requires correct location codes and a color scale. Use z for the numeric field.
entries.common_bug: Using the wrong locationmode for your identifiers.

entries.title: Create an indicator trace
entries.problem: Show a KPI or single numeric status.
entries.trigger: When dashboard summaries need a compact metric tile.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Indicator(mode="number+delta", value=82, delta={"reference": 75}, title={"text": "Conversion"}))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Indicator traces are ideal for KPI display. Keep the number of indicators small.
entries.common_bug: Using an indicator when time-series context is still required.

entries.title: Create a table trace
entries.problem: Display structured tabular output inside a figure.
entries.trigger: When a chart needs an embedded report table.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Table(
    header=dict(values=["A", "B"]),
    cells=dict(values=[[1, 2, 3], ["x", "y", "z"]])
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Table is a domain trace. It works well in dashboards and summaries.
entries.common_bug: Using Table for large datasets instead of a data grid.

entries.title: Create a candlestick chart
entries.problem: Show OHLC price movements.
entries.trigger: When financial time-series data is open-high-low-close.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Candlestick(
    x=["2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03"],
    open=[100, 110, 105],
    high=[120, 115, 110],
    low=[90, 100, 95],
    close=[110, 105, 108]
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Candlestick is the standard OHLC trace. Use datetime axes when possible.
entries.common_bug: Misordering open, high, low, and close arrays.

entries.title: Create a waterfall chart
entries.problem: Show cumulative increases and decreases.
entries.trigger: When a sequence of deltas leads to a total.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Waterfall(
    x=["Revenue", "Costs", "Taxes", "Profit"],
    y=[100, -40, -10, 50]
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Waterfall is the standard delta trace. Use it for financial or operational decomposition.
entries.common_bug: Mixing pre-aggregated totals and step changes incorrectly.

entries.title: Create a funnel trace
entries.problem: Show a staged pipeline with decreasing values.
entries.trigger: When a process narrows through stages.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Funnel(y=["Visit", "Signup", "Trial", "Paid"], x=[1, 2, 3]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Funnel traces are compact for progression analysis. Keep the stage order deliberate.
entries.common_bug: Reordering stages and changing the funnel meaning.

entries.title: Create a pie trace
entries.problem: Show simple composition.
entries.trigger: When the number of categories is small.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Pie(labels=["A", "B", "C"], values=[10, 20, 30]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Pie is for simple part-to-whole summaries. Use it sparingly.
entries.common_bug: Using pie charts for many categories.

entries.title: Create a sunburst trace
entries.problem: Show hierarchy in a radial layout.
entries.trigger: When tree structure must be compactly displayed.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Sunburst(labels=["A", "B", "C"], parents=["", "A", "A"], values=[10, 20, 30]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Sunburst is a domain trace for hierarchy. Parent relationships must be correct.
entries.common_bug: Building inconsistent parent-child relationships.

entries.title: Create a treemap trace
entries.problem: Show hierarchy as nested rectangles.
entries.trigger: When dense hierarchical structure needs a compact display.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Treemap(labels=["A", "B", "C"], parents=["", "A", "A"], values=[10, 20, 30]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Treemap is useful for compact hierarchical summaries. Keep labels short.
entries.common_bug: Overloading the treemap with too many sibling nodes.

entries.title: Create an icicle trace
entries.problem: Show hierarchy in a top-down layout.
entries.trigger: When hierarchical levels need visual separation.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Icicle(labels=["A", "B", "C"], parents=["", "A", "A"], values=[10, 20, 30]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Icicle is the rectangular hierarchy companion to sunburst. It works well for level inspection.
entries.common_bug: Expecting it to behave like a flat categorical bar chart.

entries.title: Create a sankey diagram
entries.problem: Show weighted flow between nodes.
entries.trigger: When movement between stages or systems matters.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Sankey(
    node=dict(label=["A", "B", "C"]),
    link=dict(source=[0, 1, 0], target=[2, 2, 1], value=[10, 20, 15])
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Sankey is ideal for flow and allocation analysis. Keep node labels clear.
entries.common_bug: Mismatching source and target indices.

entries.title: Style marker appearance
entries.problem: Control point size, color, and symbol.
entries.trigger: When trace styling must match a design system.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6],
    mode="markers",
    marker=dict(size=12, color="royalblue", symbol="circle")
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: marker is the main point-style container. Keep palette choices consistent.
entries.common_bug: Setting incompatible symbol or size values for the intended trace.

entries.title: Style line appearance
entries.problem: Control stroke width, dash, and color.
entries.trigger: When line encoding must be visually distinct.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6],
    mode="lines",
    line=dict(width=3, dash="dash", color="black")
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: line styling belongs on line-capable traces. Use dash patterns sparingly.
entries.common_bug: Applying line styling to traces that do not draw lines.

entries.title: Control fill and opacity
entries.problem: Shade the area under or between traces.
entries.trigger: When the chart needs stronger area emphasis.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6],
    fill="tozeroy",
    opacity=0.5,
    mode="lines"
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: fill and opacity work well together. Keep opacity low enough to preserve context.
entries.common_bug: Making filled regions too opaque and hiding geometry.

entries.title: Use hovertemplate
entries.problem: Define precise hover text.
entries.trigger: When default hover text is too verbose or incomplete.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter( x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], customdata=["a", "b", "c"], hovertemplate="x=%{x}
y=%{y}
tag=%{customdata}" )) fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: hovertemplate overrides hoverinfo. Use <extra></extra> to hide the secondary box.
entries.common_bug: Leaving the default extra box visible when it is not wanted.

entries.title: Attach customdata
entries.problem: Carry extra per-point metadata for interaction or callbacks.
entries.trigger: When hover or click logic needs hidden fields.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=[1, 2, 3],
    y=[4, 5, 6],
    customdata=[["u1"], ["u2"], ["u3"]],
    hovertemplate="id=%{customdata}<extra></extra>"
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: customdata is the standard payload channel for interactivity. It pairs naturally with hovertemplate.
entries.common_bug: Assuming customdata is visible without referencing it in templates or callbacks.

entries.title: Control colorbars
entries.problem: Tune numeric color legends for continuous traces.
entries.trigger: When color mapping needs explicit labeling or placement.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6],
    mode="markers",
    marker=dict(
        size=12,
        color=[1, 2, 3],
        colorscale="Viridis",
        colorbar=dict(title="Value")
    )
))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: colorbar belongs to continuous color encodings. Label it clearly.
entries.common_bug: Leaving an unlabeled colorbar in stakeholder-facing output.

entries.title: Set legend grouping
entries.problem: Tie traces together for legend toggling.
entries.trigger: When multiple traces should hide and show as a unit.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A1", legendgroup="A"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="A2", legendgroup="A")
])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: legendgroup is useful for linked trace families. It improves legend hygiene.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to give grouped traces the same legendgroup.

entries.title: Control visibility states
entries.problem: Hide a trace while keeping it in the legend.
entries.trigger: When a trace should be optional at load time.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure([
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="visible"),
    go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], name="hidden", visible="legendonly"),
])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: visible='legendonly' hides the trace but preserves legend access. This is common in dashboards.
entries.common_bug: Using invisible traces when the legend item should still be available.

entries.title: Control click mode
entries.problem: Configure legend and point-click interactions.
entries.trigger: When the app depends on chart click behavior.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.update_layout(clickmode="event+select")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: clickmode affects selection and click events. Use it when building interactive workflows.
entries.common_bug: Assuming clicks and selections are enabled by default for every renderer.

entries.title: Enable selection-friendly traces
entries.problem: Prepare a scatter for point selection workflows.
entries.trigger: When downstream code needs selected points.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], mode="markers"))
fig.update_traces(selected=dict(marker=dict(opacity=1.0)), unselected=dict(marker=dict(opacity=0.2)))
fig.update_layout(dragmode="lasso")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: selected and unselected styles matter in analytical apps. Use lasso or box selection deliberately.
entries.common_bug: Styling selection but forgetting to enable a selection dragmode.

entries.title: Show a figure
entries.problem: Render the current figure interactively.
entries.trigger: When you need notebook or browser display.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: show uses the configured renderer. It is the standard display method.
entries.common_bug: Expecting show to create a saved file automatically.

entries.title: Write HTML output
entries.problem: Save an interactive standalone file.
entries.trigger: When the chart must be shared without Python.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.write_html("figure.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
entries.minimal_notes: HTML export is the safest share format. CDN mode reduces file size.
entries.common_bug: Using CDN output in offline environments.

entries.title: Write a static image
entries.problem: Export a PNG or other static asset.
entries.trigger: When reports or slide decks need fixed images.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
fig.write_image("figure.png", scale=2)
entries.minimal_notes: Static image export requires a supported export backend. Use scale to increase resolution.
entries.common_bug: Attempting image export without the required renderer/backend installed.

entries.title: Convert to HTML string
entries.problem: Embed a figure in a custom app or template.
entries.trigger: When the output needs to be injected into HTML.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go

fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6]))
html = fig.to_html(include_plotlyjs="cdn", full_html=False)
print(html[:200])
entries.minimal_notes: to_html is useful for integration pipelines. It returns a string, not a file.
entries.common_bug: Treating to_html like a file-writing method.

entries.title: Add animation sliders
entries.problem: Let users navigate between frames.
entries.trigger: When frame playback needs direct control.
entries.minimal_notes: sliders map frame names to actions. Keep step labels short.
entries.common_bug: Naming frames inconsistently with slider step targets.

entries.title: Add play/pause buttons
entries.problem: Control animation playback.
entries.trigger: When users need to start or stop an animated figure.
entries.minimal_notes: updatemenus is the standard animation control surface. Keep button actions explicit.
entries.common_bug: Building controls without matching frame names or animation args.

entries.title: Use Scattergl for large point sets
entries.problem: Improve performance for dense scatter plots.
entries.trigger: When SVG scatter becomes too slow.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

n = 50000
fig = go.Figure(go.Scattergl(x=np.random.randn(n), y=np.random.randn(n), mode="markers"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scattergl uses WebGL rendering. It is the standard large-scatter option.
entries.common_bug: Assuming Scattergl is always better than Scatter for every chart.

entries.title: Reduce plotting cost with simpler traces
entries.problem: Keep large figures responsive.
entries.trigger: When many traces or points slow down rendering.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(10000)
y = np.sin(x / 100.0)
fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(x=x[::10], y=y[::10], mode="lines"))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Downsampling is often the fastest optimization. Simplify traces before adding more layout complexity.
entries.common_bug: Trying to render every raw point when a sampled view is enough.

entries.title: Preserve rendering strategy for large datasets
entries.problem: Choose a stable approach for high-volume figures.
entries.trigger: When interactive performance matters in production.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import numpy as np

n = 100000
fig = go.Figure(go.Scattergl(x=np.random.randn(n), y=np.random.randn(n), mode="markers", marker=dict(opacity=0.4)))
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_white")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: WebGL is a rendering strategy, not a full data-management solution. Combine it with aggregation when needed.
entries.common_bug: Relying on WebGL while leaving data volume and hover payload unchanged.

entries.title: Create a distribution plot
entries.problem: Build a compact distribution figure from sample data.
entries.trigger: When a quick legacy helper is acceptable.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.figure_factory as ff

fig = ff.create_distplot([[1, 2, 1.5, 2.5, 3]], ["sample"])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Figure factory helpers are compact utilities, not the main API. Use them only when they fit the task.
entries.common_bug: Treating figure_factory as the preferred long-term composition API.

entries.title: Create an annotated heatmap
entries.problem: Show a matrix with text labels.
entries.trigger: When cell values must be visible directly.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.figure_factory as ff

fig = ff.create_annotated_heatmap([[1, 2, 3], ], x=["A", "B"], y=["R1", "R2"])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Annotated heatmaps are useful for small matrices. Keep text readable.
entries.common_bug: Using annotated heatmaps for large matrices and overwhelming the view.

entries.title: Create a quiver plot
entries.problem: Visualize vector direction and magnitude.
entries.trigger: When flow fields or directional vectors matter.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.figure_factory as ff

fig = ff.create_quiver(x=[1, 2, 3], y=[4, 5, 6], u=[1, -1], v=[0.5, 0.8, 1.0])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Quiver is a compact vector-field helper. It is useful for directional data.
entries.common_bug: Using quiver when a scatter or line trace is sufficient.

entries.title: Create a table with figure factory
entries.problem: Generate a quick table figure.
entries.trigger: When a simple table helper is enough.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.figure_factory as ff

fig = ff.create_table([[1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: The helper is compact and fast for simple tables. Prefer go.Table for direct trace work.
entries.common_bug: Using figure_factory tables for highly customized reporting layouts.

quick_references.title: Common subplot options
rows: Enable right-side y-axis in xy subplot.

common_errors.error: Mismatched coordinate dimensions on custom traces.
common_errors.cause: Passing arrays of differing lengths to x and y coordinates in Scatter or similar traces, leading to trace rendering failure.
common_errors.solution: Ensure that the lists or numpy arrays mapped to coordinates have identical dimensions.

common_errors.error: Secondary y-axis does not display or align.
common_errors.cause: Failing to configure secondary_y=True inside the specs array of make_subplots, or adding traces without secondary_y.
common_errors.solution: Initialize subplots with secondary_y=True in the specs parameter, and set secondary_y=True/False when adding traces.

common_errors.error: Layout configurations overwrite previously set properties.
common_errors.cause: Repeatedly calling update_layout with basic dictionary overrides instead of utilizing nested parameter paths.
common_errors.solution: Use dot-notation parameter names (e.g., legend_title_text='Group') or merge nested dictionary structures.

common_errors.error: Trace modifications target the wrong subplots.
common_errors.cause: Failing to pass row and col values to add_trace or update_traces, resulting in global overlays or missing plots.
common_errors.solution: Always specify the precise row and col index when interacting with a subplot figure layout.

common_errors.cause: Source and target indices refer to non-existent nodes, or node labels are improperly sized.
common_errors.solution: Map source and target vectors to valid 0-indexed integers representing the indices in the node label array.

performance_checklist.recommendations: Use Scattergl instead of Scatter for plots exceeding 5,000 markers to leverage GPU WebGL rendering speed.
Limit grid coordinates and triangle counts in Mesh3d and Surface traces to keep browser interactions responsive.
Pre-aggregate or slice large time series data sets using slice step notation (e.g., x[::10]) before passing them to low-level traces.
Always reuse figure structures or clear plots explicitly when generating visualizations in server loops to manage WebGL context leaks.

production_checklist: Verify all subplot cells map exactly to the configured specs grid layout.
Use layout.hovermode='x unified' for dense multi-line time series charts to ease comparisons.
Clean hover readouts completely using customdata and explicit hovertemplate rules.
Define explicit figure canvas height and width dimensions for predictable grid aspect ratios.
Check that contrast between paper_bgcolor and plot_bgcolor fits standard dark/light design systems.
Group multiple traces using legendgroup to allow users to toggle them as a single logical block.
